thread.title: Lattice Semiconductor Looking To Go From Stabilization To Growth - Lattice Semiconductor Corporation (NASDAQ:LSCC)

author: Stephen Simpson, CFA
title: Lattice Semiconductor Looking To Go From Stabilization To Growth - Lattice Semiconductor Corporation (NASDAQ:LSCC)
text:
It has been a rocky couple of years for Lattice Semiconductor ( LSCC ), including a failed attempt to sell the company to a Chinese entity, but the company has regrouped and management has stabilized the business. Now the question moves to whether or not the company’s focus on lower-cost, lower-power FPGAs for applications like robotics, security/surveillance, auto ADAS, and edge computing/networking can drive a re-acceleration to double-digit revenue growth and meaningful margin leverage.
I’m skeptical on Lattice’s prospects for attaining/maintaining double-digit revenue growth on any consistent or long-term basis, but I do believe the company’s low-power FPGA and millimeter wave technologies address real market needs and opportunities, and I believe the move to 28nm FD-SOI chip architecture can drive meaningful margin leverage. With the shares trading between my DCF and margin-based EV/revenue fair values, I believe there’s still upside here, but Lattice will need to start delivering some beat-and-raise quarters to drive truly exciting performance.
Industrial And Auto Leading The Way For several quarters now, Lattice’s highest-margin segment has also been its best grower. Lattice generates substantially better gross margins in its Industrial & Auto segment, and that’s also where the company has been seeing the best sales results recently, with Q4’17 yoy growth of 7% accelerating to 20% in the first quarter of this year on good sales to robotics and security/surveillance customers.
Machine vision is a significant market opportunity for Lattice’s low-power FPGAs, as is human-machine interface (or HMI) and other factory automation functions, and the healthy global demand for robotics and factory automation is fueling this business.
I also expect the auto market to be an emerging growth opportunity for Lattice in the coming years. While Lattice is not looking to compete in the high-end FPGA auto applications like autonomous driving, there are still opportunities in applications like “image stitching,” where Lattice’s chips can take the images of multiple separate cameras and present them as a single continuous image. I would also expect to see growing opportunities for Lattice’s millimeter wave technology in both industrial and auto applications, as it can replace connectors and offer meaningful bandwidth at low power.
How Much Can “Edge” Contribute? Lattice has also been talking up its potential in so-called edge applications. At the risk of oversimplification, Lattice is focusing on chips and technologies for the devices that work at the edge of cloud/wireless networks – smart home/connected home devices, AR/VR, and other devices that are basically the “business end” of connected systems.
Lattice’s sales pitch is really built around low-cost, low-power devices that can handle a lot of independent functions and take some of the load off the network. FPGAs can work as the main processor for some simple edge devices and the company’s chips allow for functional, semi-autonomous operations – surveillance systems can activate themselves when a stimulus is received, take/process images, and send them along to the network.
Those same functionalities are also useful in applications like factory robotics/automation, where robots in manufacturing/assembly and warehouse functions are increasingly tasked with more complicated “read and react” duties that require onboard image recognition, processing, and communication capabilities.
How much these opportunities can/will contribute to Lattice is an open question, and I don’t expect to see a major impact for a few years. Still, between surveillance/security, robotics, and AR/VR, I can see worthwhile market opportunities for a company of Lattice’s size – particularly as these applications will require high flexibility and reliability but lower power demands.
A New Process On The Way Lattice will apparently start taping out designs for its 28nm FD-SOI process later this year, which is a little sooner than I expected. I’ve written about FD-SOI before, but I’ll repeat some of the highlights. FD-SOI is a chip design alternative to Fin-FET that can be exceptionally power-efficient and cost-effective compared to smaller Fin-FET nodes. Although the substrates are more expensive, it requires fewer patterning steps.
While FD-SOI isn’t the right approach for all chips, I believe it will be a compelling opportunity for Lattice’s more price-sensitive target markets, and I believe FD-SOI adoption can drive greater revenue growth and simultaneously attractive margins for the company. I’d also note that STMicroelectronics ( STM ) and NXP Semiconductors ( NXPI ) have gotten on board with 22nm/28nm FD-SOI as well.
The Bottom Line Between serious issues in the business, an unsuccessful attempt to sell the company, and most recently the expansion of the board and the retirement of the CEO, Lattice has been through a lot over the past couple of years. Recent weakness in Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) handset volumes certainly hasn’t helped, but growth in the industrial/auto business has helped offset that and I believe Lattice has more or less stabilized the business and has done so at a level where it still generates positive free cash flow.
Now the question is whether Lattice’s strategic priorities and foci can drive an acceleration in the business with both revenue growth and margin leverage. As Microsemi (recently acquired by Microchip ( MCHP )) showed, there is demand out there for lower-end FPGAs that don’t try to match up to the capabilities of what Xilinx ( XLNX ) and Intel ( INTC ) offer, but still offer the same basic advantages of FPGAs (including design/programming flexibility, faster design cycles, and good performance in highly parallelized tasks). Given the growing need for more capable edge devices (but with meaningful limitations on power consumption and cost), I think there’s a real market there for Lattice. Now it’s a question of execution.
I’m looking for long-term revenue growth on the higher end of the mid-single digits, and I’m expecting a significant ramp in FCF generation over the next decade (into the mid-to-high teens). I believe that Lattice will still have some diseconomies of scale, though, and I can see Lattice as a buyout target for a company that wants that FPGA technology and can leverage production and operating costs.
The Bottom Line I believe Lattice’s fair value is between the mid-$6s up to around $8 today, with my DCF model on the lower end of the range and my EV/revenue model (driven largely by margins) at the higher end. I like to buy chip stocks below my DCF fair value when I can, and sell as they close in on the EV/revenue fair value. To that end, Lattice is only a little above my DCF fair value and while there are still significant operating risks here, I think these shares are worth a look from more aggressive, risk-tolerant investors.
